summary.text: When Athens owed Minos a tribute of youths for the Minotaur, Theseus sailed on the black-sailed ship, won Ariadne's love and Daedalus' secret of the labyrinth, killed the beast with his fists, and fled Crete — but left the princess on Naxos and forgot the white sail, so Aegeus cast himself into the sea.

chapters.title: The tribute to Minos
chapters.text: Androgeus, son of Minos, had been killed at Athens — some say by the Marathonian bull, others by jealous competitors — and the Cretan king imposed a tribute: every nine years seven youths and seven maidens sent to the labyrinth for the Minotaur. Theseus offered himself among the third company, or was chosen by lot; Aegeus gave him a black sail and charged him to hoist white canvas if he returned alive.

chapters.title: The Cyclades answer Minos
chapters.text: Before the tribute sailed, Minos mustered the Cyclades against Athens. Ovid names the allies who agreed to aid: level Myconos, the chalky fields of Kimolos, Syros covered with wild thyme, level Seriphos, Paros of marble cliffs, and Siphnos — the place Arne the impious Siphnian had betrayed for gold and was changed into a black-foot daw. When tidings of Androgeus' death reached Minos as he sacrificed to the Graces in Paros, he threw away his garland and stopped the flute-music, though he finished the rite — hence, Apollodorus says, the island long sacrificed to the Graces without flutes or garlands.

chapters.title: The clew of thread
chapters.text: At Knossos, Ariadne, daughter of Minos, fell in love with the Athenian and promised help if he would take her away. Daedalus — the artificer who built the maze — gave her the plan: let the hero unwind a clew of thread as he went in, so he could find the way back. Theseus entered the labyrinth, met the Minotaur, and killed it with his bare hands; he drew the thread after him and came out with the youths and maidens of Athens.

chapters.title: Naxos and the black sail
chapters.text: They sailed by night and put in at Naxos — Homer's sea-girt Dia — where Dionysus carried Ariadne off. Grieving, Theseus forgot to spread the white sail. Aegeus, watching from the acropolis, saw only black canvas and cast himself into the sea; the hero returned king of a fatherless city. The poets tell Ariadne's end apart: Homer says Artemis slew her on Dionysus' testimony; Hesiod makes her Dionysus' immortal wife; Apollodorus has the god wedded her on Naxos after Theseus abandoned her.
